title: Linking two events
goal: Linking sentences with *-ж*, *-аад* and *-вал* — three suffixes that turn short sentences into a story.
bekal: link two events in sequence with *-аад*
express manner and simultaneous actions with *-ж / -ч*

dialogs.title: Яриа — Байр хайж байна
dialogs.intro: Budi wants to move from the dorm into a small apartment. Sarnai helps him call the landlord.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Budi, what kind of apartment are you looking for?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: One room and close to campus would be good.
lines.literal: one room-with, school-from near if-is good.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: How many tugriks can you pay a month?
lines.literal: month's how-many tugrik up-to pay-ing able Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: About seven hundred thousand. More than that would be hard.
lines.literal: seven hundred thousand about. more price-with if hard.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: OK, let's look at the ads and then call. Here's a good one.
lines.literal: OK, ad look-after let's-call. this one nice is.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Good afternoon. I'm calling about your ad. Is the apartment still for rent?
lines.literal: well is Q. ad see-after call-ing is. apartment for-rent Q?

lines.speaker: Эзэн:
lines.id: Yes, it is. One room, a kitchen, and a bathroom.
lines.literal: yes, is-being. one room, fire pot, wash's room-with.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: How much is the rent? Are bills included?
lines.literal: rent how-much Q? bill included Q?

lines.speaker: Эзэн:
lines.id: Six hundred thousand a month. Electricity and water are extra.
lines.literal: month-in six hundred thousand. electricity, water separate.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Can we see it? Could we come this evening?
lines.literal: see-ing may Q? today evening-at-own if-arrive may Q?

lines.speaker: Эзэн:
lines.id: Yes. Come at seven. I'll send you the address.
lines.literal: may. seven hour-at come-please. address let's-send.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Thank you! After we see the apartment, if we like it, let's sign the contract tomorrow.
lines.literal: thanks! apartment-object see-after, if-liked tomorrow contract let's-make.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: No need to rush. Better to see two or three apartments first and then decide.
lines.literal: hurry-after need-not. two, three apartment see-after decide -the better.

notes: ⚠️ **Three linking suffixes, three sharply different meanings:** *-ж / -ч* means "while, by way of"; *-аад / -ээд* means "and then, after"; *-вал / -вэл* means "if". All three attach to verbs that are **not** the last verb of the sentence.

**Зар үзээд залгаж байна = "saw the ad and then am calling".** Notice that only the **last** verb gets a tense suffix; every verb before it takes a linking suffix. That's how Mongolian strings events together, and it can go on as long as you like.

**Таалагдвал = "if (it's) liked", from таалагдах + -вал.** The *-вал* suffix attaches straight to the verb root. ⚠️ For verbs ending in certain consonants, the form is *-бал / -бэл*: *ав* → *авбал* (if you take).

**Бол also means "if", but it's a separate word placed after a noun or adjective.** *Илүү үнэтэй **бол** хэцүү* = if it's more expensive, it's hard. Compare *-вал*, which attaches to verbs. The two are often used together without any trouble.
**Байна уу? on the phone means "hello?"** — literally "is (someone) there?", asking whether anyone is on the other end. Much like English "hello, anyone there?"

grammars.title: The three linking suffixes
body: This table is the heart of the unit and worth reading twice. Look at the last column: the difference between the three isn't about grammar but about **how the two events relate**.

head: Suffix
Example
Meaning
How they relate
rows: At the same time, or manner.
In sequence; the first finishes first.
If you go, let me know.
If I have money, I'll buy it.
When you enter the house, take off your shoes.
At the same time, a point in time.
As soon as you arrive, call me.

after: ⚠️ **Tell -ж from -аад with one question: does the first event finish before the second begins?** If yes, use *-аад*. If both happen at once, or the first describes **how** the second is done, use *-ж*. *Идээд явсан* = ate first, then left. *Идэж явсан* = left while eating.

**A Mongolian sentence can chain five or six verbs in a row this way**, and only the last one marks the tense. *Босоод, цай уугаад, хувцасаа өмсөөд, ажилдаа явлаа* = "Got up, drank tea, got dressed, then went to work." This is the signature sound of Mongolian, and it sounds natural precisely because it's long.

grammars.title: Forming the linking suffixes
body: All of them are built from the verb root (the dictionary form without *-х*), and the vowel follows the harmony you already know.
after: ⚠️ **-ч replaces -ж after в, г, р, с and after long vowels.** *Авах* → *авч* (not *авж*); *өгөх* → *өгч*. Say both aloud and you'll pick the right one — the wrong form really is hard to pronounce.
**To make a condition negative, use *-хгүй бол*:** *Мөнгө байхгүй бол авахгүй* = if there's no money, I won't buy it. This is the form you'll hear most for negative conditions.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Халаалт is the word that decides how comfortable your life in Ulaanbaatar will be.** Most city apartments are connected to central heating that's switched on around September 15 and off around May 15 — **with no thermostat inside the home**. If you're renting, ask *халаалттай юу?* An apartment without central heating in Mongolia isn't a lifestyle choice but a risk.

blocks.title: Дүүрэг and хороо: how addresses work in Ulaanbaatar
items: Ulaanbaatar is divided into *дүүрэг* (districts), then *хороо* (subdistricts), then building and door numbers.
Sample address: *Сүхбаатар дүүрэг, 1-р хороо, 25-р байр, 34 тоот*.
⚠️ **Street names are hardly used in conversation.** People give directions by landmarks: the name of a building, a bus stop or a shop.
If you order a taxi or send a parcel, have a **landmark** ready, not an address — something like "behind the supermarket, just before the mosque".

blocks.text: Read this paragraph aloud twice. It has seven verbs in a row, and only the last one marks the tense — this is what Mongolian really sounds like, and once you can say it without stumbling, you've crossed the biggest hurdle of A1.

blocks.title: Өнөөдрийн минь өдөр
items: *Өглөө зургаан цаг хагаст босоод,* — Got up at half past six in the morning, then
*нүүрээ угаагаад, цай уугаад,* — washed my face, drank tea,
*хувцасаа өмсөөд, гэрээсээ гараад,* — got dressed, left the house,
*автобусанд сууж сургуульдаа очлоо.* — took the bus and got to campus.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: If we have time, let's meet.
If it rains, I won't go out.
Call me as soon as you arrive.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice the pair **эхлэх / дуусах** (start / end) and **дуусгах** (to finish something). The suffix **-га / -гэ** turns a "happens by itself" verb into a "makes it happen" verb: *дуусах* (to end) → *дуусгах* (to finish something); *босох* (to get up) → *босгох* (to wake someone up); *сурах* (to learn) → *сургах* (to teach). It's like English pairs such as "rise / raise" or "fall / fell", only fully regular — and very productive.

items: If we have time, let's meet.
If it rains, I won't go out.
